hints: Look at what triglycerides and phospholipids both contain, a glycerol backbone plus fatty acid tails made of long hydrocarbon chains.
Think about how fatty acids can vary (with or without C=C double bonds) and how the number of ester bonds and the overall polarity differ between the two lipids.
walkthrough:
**Recall both structures side by side**

Think of them as cousins. Both are built on one glycerol molecule with fatty acids attached by ester bonds.

Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Phospholipid = glycerol + 2 fatty acids + 1 phosphate group.

**Focus on the hydrocarbon tails**

The fatty acids in both lipids are long hydrocarbon chains. In biology, any fatty acid can be saturated (only single C-C bonds, no C=C) or unsaturated (one or more C=C double bonds).

This variation applies equally to triglycerides and to phospholipids.

**Check why the other features are not shared**

Phosphate on glycerol, overall polarity, and three ester bonds are not the same in both. Only the nature of the fatty acid chains is a true shared feature, so B is correct.

options.A: Only phospholipids have a phosphate group joined to glycerol. Triglycerides have three fatty acids and no phosphate.
options.B: Both contain fatty acids with hydrocarbon chains, and in both lipids those chains can be saturated with no double bonds or unsaturated with double bonds.
options.C: Triglycerides are non-polar and hydrophobic overall. Phospholipids have a polar hydrophilic head plus non-polar tails, so they are not both polar molecules.
options.D: Only triglycerides have three ester bonds. Phospholipids have two ester bonds to the two fatty acids, plus a different linkage to phosphate.
